sources.content_summary: npm trusted publishing is package-side configuration using short-lived OIDC credentials; stage-only permission and token denial provide the strongest boundary, but configuration errors can remain latent until a publish attempt.
key_points: A workflow file cannot prove the package-side trusted-publisher relationship exists.
Trusted publishing can automatically generate provenance for public packages from public repositories.
Stage-only permission still requires maintainer review and approval.
misconceptions: A valid GitHub workflow proves npm trusted publishing is configured.
OIDC removes the need for package-side authorization.

sources.content_summary: npm staging is a live registry operation for existing packages and requires a later 2FA-protected approval before public availability.
key_points: New packages cannot use staged publishing.
Staging is not equivalent to an offline rehearsal.
Approval is an independent human-authority event.
misconceptions: A dry-run proves npm staging works.
An rc dist-tag is the same mechanism as staged publishing.

sources.content_summary: GitHub artifact attestations require explicit workflow permissions and actions/attest, and are created only by an executed workflow over concrete subjects.
key_points: The workflow needs contents read, id-token write, and attestations write.
A repository workflow contract is not an emitted attestation.
misconceptions: Referencing actions/attest in YAML proves an attestation exists.

sources.content_summary: pub.dev automated publishing must be configured by an uploader or publisher administrator and binds repository, tag pattern, and optionally a GitHub environment.
key_points: Repository inspection cannot prove pub.dev account-side configuration.
The pubspec version and pushed tag must match the configured pattern.
Environment protection can be bound into the OIDC identity.
misconceptions: A successful local pub dry-run proves automated publishing authority.
Any tag can publish once id-token write is present.

sources.content_summary: cargo publish dry-run performs verification without upload; real publication needs registry authentication and can time out while index visibility is still pending.
key_points: Dry-run is local package verification, not registry acceptance.
A publish timeout does not necessarily mean upload failure and requires registry inspection.
misconceptions: A green cargo publish dry-run proves crates.io ownership.
A publish timeout is safe to retry blindly.
